Packaging and labelling operations require particular attention because a correct medicine
in the wrong pack or with the wrong label can put
patients at risk. Controls should protect product identity, strength, batch information
and instructions. A packaging error may result in a patient receiving
incorrect strength information or directions for use. Specific packaging controls depend
on the product, market and approved procedures.
Printed packaging materials should be approved, identified, stored and issued under
appropriate controls. Different products, strengths and markets may have similar-looking artwork.
Controlled issuance and secure storage reduce the chance of a mix-up.
Obsolete or superseded printed components must be prevented from unintended use.
Reconciliation and destruction practices should follow approved site procedures.
Before starting a packaging batch, line clearance helps verify that unrelated
product, printed components, labels and documents from previous operations are removed
or appropriately controlled. Equipment and area status should be confirmed. The
line-clearance procedure should define responsibilities and records. A completed checklist is
meaningful only when the physical checks were actually performed.
During packaging, checks may verify the correct product, printed component, batch
number, expiry information, readability and packaging integrity. The appropriate checks, frequency
and acceptance criteria must be defined by the approved process. Camera
inspection or barcode verification may provide additional controls, but automated systems
still require suitable qualification, maintenance and oversight.
Serialization can assign a unique identifier to saleable packs where required
by the applicable market. Aggregation may associate packs with cartons and
shippers. These systems support traceability and verification but do not replace
basic GMP controls. Regulatory requirements vary by jurisdiction and product, so
the site must follow the relevant market-specific rules and validated system
design.
Packaging reconciliation compares quantities issued, used, rejected, returned and otherwise accounted
for. Unexplained discrepancies, particularly involving printed materials or finished packs, should
be investigated according to approved procedures. Reconciliation tolerances, if applicable, must
be scientifically and procedurally justified. Any unexplained quantity difference must be
evaluated before batch disposition under approved procedures.
Mix-up prevention is strongest when multiple controls work together. These can
include physical segregation, material identification, approved artwork, line clearance, in-process checks,
barcode systems and independent review. Each layer reduces a different failure
opportunity. A single final inspection is not an adequate substitute for
controlling risks throughout packaging operations.
Imagine that an operator notices a carton printed for a different
strength at the packaging line. The operator should secure the operation
and report the finding under site procedures. Authorized personnel should assess
the extent of possible mix-up, affected materials and batches, and any
required investigation. Packaging should resume only after the issue is appropriately
resolved and documented. The goal is to protect patient safety and
preserve traceability.
